whatIs: Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition that can affect the skin, mucous membranes, hair, and nails. It is characterized by purplish, itchy, flat-topped bumps on the skin, and white, lacy patches in the mouth. This condition is not contagious, meaning it cannot be passed from one person to another. It most commonly occurs in middle-aged adults, though anyone can develop it. The rash may appear suddenly or develop gradually over several months, often causing significant discomfort and affecting the patient's quality of life. The exact appearance can vary depending on which part of the body is affected.

On the skin, lichen planus typically presents as intensely itchy, violaceous or purple-colored bumps. These lesions are often polygonal in shape and have a shiny surface when viewed under light. They most frequently appear on the inner wrists, forearms, lower legs, and ankles. In some cases, fine white lines, known as Wickham striae, can be seen on the surface of the bumps. The itching associated with these skin lesions can range from mild to severe, often becoming worse at night and interfering with sleep. Scratching the lesions can sometimes lead to the development of new bumps in the scratched area, a phenomenon known as the Koebner response.

When lichen planus affects the oral cavity, it usually appears as a network of raised, white, lacy patterns on the inside of the cheeks, gums, or tongue. This form is often painless but can sometimes cause a burning sensation, especially when eating spicy or acidic foods. Erosive oral lichen planus, a more severe form, involves painful ulcers and red, swollen tissues, which can make eating and drinking quite difficult. The condition can also affect the nails, leading to thinning, ridging, or even complete loss of the nail plate. Hair loss can occur if the scalp is involved, which may sometimes be permanent if scarring takes place.

The diagnosis of lichen planus is usually made through a clinical examination by a healthcare professional. In some instances, a skin biopsy may be recommended to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other conditions with similar appearances, such as eczema or psoriasis. Blood tests might also be conducted to check for underlying issues, particularly hepatitis C, which has been associated with an increased risk of developing lichen planus in some individuals. Understanding the widespread nature of the condition and its various manifestations is crucial for developing an appropriate management strategy tailored to the individual's specific symptoms and needs.
causes: The exact cause of lichen planus remains largely unknown, but it is widely considered to be an autoimmune or immune-mediated condition. In an autoimmune response, the body's immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy cells. In the case of lichen planus, the immune system targets the cells of the skin or mucous membranes. This abnormal immune reaction triggers inflammation and the subsequent development of the characteristic lesions. It is not entirely clear what initiates this immune system malfunction, but researchers believe that a combination of genetic predispositions and environmental triggers may play a significant role.

Certain environmental factors have been identified as potential triggers for the onset or exacerbation of lichen planus. Viral infections, particularly the hepatitis C virus, have been linked to the condition in several studies, though many people with lichen planus do not have hepatitis C. It is thought that the virus may stimulate an immune response that cross-reacts with the skin or mucosal cells. Exposure to specific chemicals, allergens, or metals, such as those used in dental amalgams, might also provoke a reaction in susceptible individuals, particularly contributing to oral lichen planus. Identifying and removing these potential triggers, when possible, can sometimes help in managing the condition.

Medications can occasionally induce a reaction that resembles lichen planus, known as a lichenoid drug eruption. Drugs commonly associated with this include certain high blood pressure medications, antimalarials, pain relievers, and medications used for heart disease. This type of reaction can occur months or even years after starting a new medication, making it challenging to identify the culprit. If a medication is suspected, consulting with a healthcare provider is essential to determine if an alternative treatment can be used. It is important never to stop taking prescribed medication without professional guidance.

Stress and emotional turmoil are increasingly recognized as significant contributing factors in many inflammatory and autoimmune conditions, including lichen planus. While stress may not directly cause the disease, it can exacerbate symptoms, trigger flare-ups, and make the condition more difficult to manage. The mind-body connection plays a crucial role in immune system regulation. Periods of high stress can weaken immune function and increase inflammation throughout the body. Therefore, addressing mental and emotional well-being is often an integral part of a comprehensive approach to managing chronic conditions like lichen planus, alongside addressing physical symptoms.
